title: An Integrated Framework of Financial Feature States, Scenario Candidates and a Lightweight Local Selection Model: A Matched-Information Comparison for S&P 500 Price-Path Selection
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support investment decisions, yet it is rarely tested whether a lightweight language model that can run inside an institution adds value over conventional learners. We integrate financial feature states, seven candidate realization types of the price path, a local language-model selector and retrieval-augmented evidence contextualization into one decision-support framework for the S&P 500 index, and compare this selector with traditional alternatives under a matched-information, leakage-controlled protocol. On the 2024onward evaluation period, the conventional baselines achieved higher macro-F1 at both horizons; financial adaptation improved the language model but did not close the gap. Its choices were sensitive to candidate order, generated reports cited identifiers outside the provided evidence, and an exploratory economic evaluation showed that it only reproduced an always-long position. The study contributes a benchmark, a comparison protocol and an explicitly reported negative result for AI-assisted scenario selection in finance.
why: Rigorous negative result: LLMs underperformed baselines for S&P 500 price prediction with proper evaluation discipline.

title: Do Markets Dream of Artificial Intelligence? Macroeconomic Effects and International Spillovers of AI News Shocks
abstract: This paper identifies AI news shocks from financial markets and traces their macroe-conomic effects in the United States and the euro area. We combine a daily equity factor based on differences in firms’ AI exposures with sign, magnitude, and narrative restrictions in a Bayesian VAR to isolate revisions in AI’s expected economic value. Monthly local projections reveal an investment-led adjustment in the US: capital-goods orders rise early and persistently, while aggregate activity responds more gradually and with greater uncertainty. Producer prices increase before consumer prices, and the expansion spreads from sectors closely connected to the AI production network to the broader economy. In the euro area, equity prices rise and the euro depreciates; import and energy costs feed into inflation before real activity strengthens. Inflation expectations and nominal rates also increase. The results highlight a monetary policy dilemma: financial spillovers and imported price pressures arrive before the broader productive gains from AI adoption.
why: Rigorous macro AI news shocks analysis, not about ML building

title: SLM-Augmented Regulatory Impact Propagation: A Lightweight Architecture for Compliance-aware Change Analysis in Legacy Banking Systems
abstract: It is challenging to perform regulatory change analysis within legacy banking environments due to interpreting new compliance requirements within the context of a complex, interconnected technological infrastructure with limited possibilities related to privacy, security, and computational resources. While Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a high level of performance related to regulatory text analysis, usage of such models through cloud-based services may raise certain concerns regarding data residency, infrastructure reliance, processing latency, and cost of computation. As an attempt to solve the problem without changing the structure of the Regulatory Impact Propagation Model (RIPM), we propose in this paper SLM-RIPM, a model that utilizes locally available Small Language Models (SLMs) and selective cloud-based LLM escalation. We start the proposed solution with the introduction of the Obligation Complexity Scorer, which evaluates the regulatory obligation by taking into account such factors as jurisdictional scope, structural complexity, systemtype specificity, and cross-regulatory interactions. Then we apply the complexity-aware router to direct Level 1-3 obligations to a local SLM and escalate Level 4-5 obligations to a cloud-based LLM. After that, we proceed with dependency graph propagation and impact scoring to determine directly and transitively affected banking systems. Our solution is validated through three different regulatory changes. The experiments carried out show that SLM-RIPM yields an accuracy of 98.30% during regulatory impact analysis while lowering the delay and overhead costs in computation and also meeting stricter data-residency requirements by doing local processing of SLMs.
why: LLM regulatory system proposal, no empirical results shown

title: Consumer Digital Twin Framework for Personalized Pricing: Behavioral Segmentation, Machine Learning, and Simulation-Based Revenue Optimization
abstract: Dynamic pricing is a fundamental challenge in e-commerce since firms are required to balance maximizing revenue with consumer heterogeneity across international markets. Advances in digital technologies have allowed businesses to adopt more data-driven approaches in order to optimize their pricing strategies. This study proposes a consumer digital twin framework combining RFM behavioral segmentation with gradient boosting demand estimation to generate personalized pricing recommendations. Using the UCI Online Retail II dataset (803,459 transactions from 39 countries) combined with World Bank GDP per capita data, we find four moderately differentiated consumer segments and estimate price elasticity for each segment. Three pricing strategies (static, elasticity-based, and digital twins) are simulated on 5859 customers. We utilize a Monte Carlo simulation to validate results and conduct three methodological analyses: theoretical justification for pricing under inelastic demand, decomposition of revenue gains into inflation and personalization effects, and synthetic validation across a range of imposed elasticity values. The digital twin model yields a 59.62% increase in revenue over static pricing where 62.6% is attributable to personalization. Furthermore, synthetic validation reveals an important boundary condition: model recommendations degrade under elastic demand unless trained on data with genuine price variation. These findings demonstrate that the integration of simulation-based personalization in enterprise pricing regimes can improve profitability and ROI without sacrificing customer satisfaction.
why: Solid pricing ML but e-commerce domain not financial markets

title: An Expert System for Cyber Insurance Incident Classification Using Large-Scale Legal Court Records
abstract: Cybersecurity incidents pose increasing challenges for organizations that depend on complex, highly interconnected systems, with the insurance sector particularly susceptible to cascading operational, legal, and financial consequences. Despite growing interest in automated incident analysis, existing studies have not adequately addressed the classification of incidents from legally documented court records, evidence that simultaneously captures technical detail and legal interpretation. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study to develop and evaluate a learning expert system for classifying cyber insurance incidents, using numerous court cases as the primary source of evidence. Unlike previous studies that rely on phishing message network traffic or synthetic benchmarks, the proposed model learns directly from these documented cyber incidents that combine organizational, technical, and legal evidence. A data-driven methodology integrates traditional machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models within a unified experimental design. Several class-balancing techniques address distributional imbalance, and model performance is evaluated through stratified cross-validation and a held-out test set. DL approaches achieved the strongest overall results, while classical models performed competitively for incident types with clearer patterns. Addressing class imbalance during training improved recall for less common incident types by more than six percentage points in several categories. These findings indicate that learning-based expert systems can support reliable and consistent cybersecurity incident classification, with direct relevance for cyber risk assessment, insurance analytics, and operational decision support.
why: Competent ML on financial services data; insurance classification not trading-facing work.

title: Ensemble Machine Learning versus Deep Learning for 15-Minute IEX Day-Ahead Market Scheduled-Volume Forecasting: Accuracy, Computational Efficiency, and Implications for India's Deviation Settlement Framework
abstract: Short-horizon electricity-market quantity forecasting is important for power-system operation under increasing renewable penetration and granular scheduling. This study compares statistical, ensemble machine-learning, and deep-learning approaches for forecasting the 15minute Final Scheduled Volume (FSV) of the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) Day-Ahead Market (DAM). FSV represents scheduled volume adjusted for real-time curtailment. The dataset spans 1 April 2022 to 9 September 2025 (approximately 119,000 observations), with comparative modelling from 1 January 2024. Meteorological variables (Delhi temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed) and calendar features are incorporated. Under a fixedwindow protocol, five models are compared: Auto-ARIMA, Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM), and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), using 1-9 September 2025 as the final holdout period. XGBoost achieves the lowest test error (MAPE 1.36%, MAE 85.38 MW, RMSE 118.69 MW) with a training time of 28.73 s, followed by RF (MAPE 2.81%, 8.62 s). Auto-ARIMA performs poorly (MAPE 30.77%), while BiLSTM and TCN are less accurate and substantially slower (MAPE 4.00% and 4.66%, respectively). N-HiTS is retained as an exploratory appendix because it uses a different rollingbacktest protocol. For the reported configuration and period, XGBoost provides the strongest accuracy-training-time trade-off, without implying general superiority of ensemble methods. The study does not quantify Deviation Settlement Mechanism (DSM) savings because this requires entity-level actual-versus-scheduled drawal/injection, applicable category, system frequency, and settlement-rate data. DSM and Just Energy Transition implications are therefore discussed as regulatory and policy implications rather than empirically established causal effects.
why: Solid method comparison on real market data; standard approach, single-country, no surprising finding.

title: An AI-Driven Cyber-Financial Resilience Framework for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises: Integrating Fraud Detection, Cyber Threat Intelligence and Risk-based Decision-making
abstract: Digital payment channels, cloud services and third-party platforms are becoming the tools of the small to midsize businesses (SMBs), but companies of this scale often aren't equipped with the tools for specialised business analytics and security employees that larger companies may possess. This gives rise to an imbalance of vulnerability that puts SMEs at a greater risk of financial fraud attacks and is increasingly automated, sometimes supported by generative artificial intelligence. This paper suggests an AI-enabled cyberfinancial resilience framework that brings together the three components: machine learning for fraud detection, fusion of cyber threat intelligence (CTI) and risk-based decision making and defines the appropriate single operational architecture for SME constraints. It is structured in three layers, each of which interacts with the other: data and sensing, AI level 2 analytics core, risk based decisions and responses, where there is also a module of explainability and a process of continuous feedback for retraining the model. The architecture is derived by carrying out a structured literature review of the current fraud detection (FD) and cyber threat intelligence (CTI) + enterprise risk management (ERM) bodies of literature, and an illustrative simulated scenario is employed to illustrate how the FD+ERM/CTI framework's fused-scoring approach can enhance detection of fraud by minimizing false-positive rates, and augment detection consistency relative to a rule-based and standalone machine-learning baselines. Governance, explainability, data quality and cost issues that arise and affect whether such a framework is feasible in resource-constrained organisations are discussed. The paper proposes a modular, adoption-friendly reference architecture that bridges three literatures which are not commonly seen together in SME-specific studies and highlights practical, ethical, and regulatory constraints to be overcome for large-scale deployment.
why: Framework paper with no concrete results or evaluation demonstrated.

title: Artificial Intelligence as an Analytical Advantage in Equity Research, Investment Decision-making, and Real-World Asset Tokenization: A Critical Appraisal
abstract: Purpose: This paper critically appraises the analytical advantages that artificial intelligence (AI), and generative large language models (LLMs) in particular, confer across three interlocking domains of contemporary digital finance: equity research, investment decisionmaking, and the emerging field of real-world asset (RWA) tokenization. Design/methodology/approach: Adopting a structured narrative-synthesis approach, the study integrates peer-reviewed empirical evidence on AI in equity markets with verified industry and preprint sources documenting the growth and technical architecture of RWA tokenization. Claims are tethered strictly to verifiable sources to avoid overstatement. Findings: AI delivers measurable advantages in information processing, predictive support, sentiment analysis, and accessibility for individual investors, while its integration into RWA tokenization enhances valuation, due diligence, risk assessment, and programmable automation. However, effects are heterogeneous and occasionally negative, and material regulatory and technical challenges remain in the tokenization domain. Originality/value: The paper bridges two literatures, AI-driven equity research and RWA tokenization, that are seldom appraised jointly, offering a disciplined, evidence-anchored assessment relevant to computer scientists, fintech engineers, and digital-finance scholars.
why: Structured narrative review of AI in finance; survey-type paper, not novel research.

title: Transforming Green Intellectual Capital into Environmental Performance: Evidence From PLS-SEM, NCA, and fsQCA
abstract: Drawing on dynamic capability theory, this study examines how green intellectual capital contributes to environmental performance in Chinese manufacturing firms. Using two-wave survey data from 417 managers, this study combines partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), necessary condition analysis (NCA), and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to capture net effects, necessary conditions, and configurational pathways of environmental performance. These three methods offer complementary evidence on symmetric effects, necessity logic, and configurational sufficiency. The PLS-SEM results indicate that green absorptive capacity mediates the relationship between green intellectual capital and environmental performance. AI-infused knowledge strengthens the conversion of green intellectual capital into green absorptive capacity by improving green knowledge processing. The NCA results suggest that green human capital, green structural capital, and green relational capital must reach minimum levels for firms to attain high environmental performance. The fsQCA results further identify multiple functionally equivalent configurations leading to high environmental performance. Beyond green knowledge resources, green absorptive capacity, AI-infused knowledge, and the configurational alignment are critical to achieving superior environmental performance. These findings advance the green intellectual capital literature by clarifying the complementary roles of these factors in driving environmental performance.
why: Off-topic: environmental management theory, not finance or LLM systems.

title: The Upside of Being Replaceable: AI, Market Structure, and Growth
abstract: I develop an endogenous-growth model in which a monopolistic AI developer supplies AI services and invests in recursive AI self-improvement. I characterize two long-run regimes under an upper bound on AI efficiency—the quantity of AI services produced per unit of compute. Complementarity between AI and labor, or a sufficiently low upper bound on AI efficiency, can leave labor as a production bottleneck. In this regime, output per worker and wages eventually grow at the exogenous rate of labor-augmenting technological progress. Instead, when AI and labor are substitutes and the upper bound is sufficiently high, an AI-dominated regime sustains permanently faster wage growth and a higher long-run return to capital. Output per worker grows faster than wages, so labor’s income share vanishes while AI-industry revenue increases as a share of output. Replacing monopoly with perfect competition eliminates private research incentives. Nevertheless, if AI is already sufficiently efficient, the competitive economy can sustain AI-dominated growth through capital accumulation and expanding AI use. By contrast, monopoly rewards research but restricts AI use through its markup. It may therefore produce more efficient AI yet slower long-run growth than competition. Numerical simulations show that early output-per-worker growth can remain moderate and similar across economies approaching different long-run regimes.
why: Pure economic theory, no data, no implementation path visible.

title: Savings and Investment Union: A New Ramp-up to the European Competitiveness Highway?
abstract: Key points: – The EU financial system is highly fragmented behind national borders. European savings suffer from a strong home bias and are held predominantly in low-risk, liquid bank deposits. Because retail banks are inherently risk-averse, they are poorly suited to funding long-term, high-risk modern technological innovations, such as artificial intelligence. – The Letta and Draghi reports call for a massive investment surge to 800 billion euros annually to reverse Europe’s economic decline. Policymakers have responded by, among other things, developing long-standing proposals for a Capital Markets Union (CMU) into a broader Savings and Investment Union (SIU). This would encompass a range of options, including granting direct authority to pan-European regulators and tax-incentivised savings accounts to encourage European households to shift from deposits to higher-risk equities. – A genuine SIU would require a European-issued safe asset to serve as a common risk-pricing benchmark and attenuate the dangerous ‘bank–sovereign doom loop’ that fuelled past euro-area debt crises. It would also attract global savings as the US dollar’s dominance weakens. – However, the political barriers to issuing a European safe asset still seem insuperable. Moreover, the supply of capital may not be the main factor currently constraining investment. Finally, the SIU raises risks of unintended consequences. It is likely to exacerbate oligopolisation of the financial industry. Shifting household savings away from bank deposits could also weaken banks’ funding base, while greater reliance on securitisation could introduce additional sources of systemic risk.
why: Policy analysis paper, not technical financial ML research.

title: Artificial intelligence innovation and employee overtime work: The moderating role of market competition
abstract: Innovation in artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming organizational processes and practices and hence exerting a profound influence on employee well-being. Market competition also plays a critical role in shaping the impact of firms' technological systems on workplace operations. Based on 3,648 Chinese listed companies from 2017 to 2023, this study empirically examines the impact of AI innovation on employee overtime work and the moderating role of market competition. The results reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship between AI innovation and overtime work, with market competition positively moderating this relationship. These findings provide empirical evidence on the complex relationship between AI innovation and employee well-being and enhance current understanding of the social impacts of AI. The results show how market competition intensity shapes the consequences of technology advancement for employee work–life balance. The study also offers guidance on how firms can improve corporate social responsibility by investing in AI.
why: Organizational study of AI impact on worker overtime

title: Problematics of Digital Technology and AI Utilization in Mathematics Learning: A Literature Review on Literacy, Access Equity, and Academic Integrity
abstract: The rapid development of digital technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) has brought significant changes to mathematics education, offering new opportunities to visualize abstract concepts, facilitate exploration, and provide rapid feedback. However, the utilization of these technologies is not without challenges. This study aims to examine the various problematics arising from the use of digital technology and AI in mathematics learning. Employing a literature review approach, this research identifies and analyzes several key issues organized into five main themes: (1) digital literacy problematics among teachers and students; (2) the digital divide in access and infrastructure; (3) the impact of AI usage on mathematical thinking abilities; (4) issues of accuracy, ethics, and academic integrity in AI usage; and (5) effective strategies for utilizing digital technology and AI. The findings indicate that while digital technology and AI possess great potential to support mathematics learning, their utilization requires careful attention to pedagogical, technical, ethical, and equity-related aspects. Technology and AI should be positioned as tools to support thinking processes, not as replacements for students' mathematical reasoning and problem-solving abilities.
why: Off-topic: mathematics education survey, not finance.
